name: Piazza Maggiore
label: Piazza Maggiore
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Torre dell'Orologio' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Torre dell'Orologio' (way/149041465): middle (16 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/12719090: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Piazza Maggiore' (161 m across).
notes: The main square of Bologna, surrounded by medieval palaces.

text.description: Piazza Maggiore has been the central meeting place of Bologna since medieval times, and it photographs well because the whole square is ringed by large historic buildings. Palazzo d'Accursio (city hall and museum) stands on the west side, with the Palazzo dei Notai to the south-west, the Basilica of San Petronio to the south-east, the Palazzo dei Banchi to the east and the Palazzo del Podestà to the north. San Petronio is the city's Duomo, and its unfinished facade is one of the easiest things to recognise in a frame. The best-regarded view looks down from the top of the clock tower, the Torre dell'Orologio, inside Palazzo d'Accursio. From there you see the square and its surrounding buildings, with a sea of red rooftops and the towers of the city beyond. The clock tower is nearby, in Palazzo d'Accursio on the west side. If you only have time for ground level, start for a wide shot of the full frontage, then go to the north-west corner. It opens into Piazza del Nettuno, where Giambologna's bronze Neptune fountain makes a good close-up with the neighbouring buildings behind it. Entry to the tower is ticketed and access can change, so check the official site before you go. Keep the lens clean and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid ledge.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, Emilia-Romagna. The square sits beside Palazzo d'Accursio, the Basilica of San Petronio and Piazza del Nettuno, which opens off its north-west corner.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Piazza Maggiore in the historic centre of Bologna. The Torre dell'Orologio is inside Palazzo d'Accursio on the western side of the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Whether you shoot from where you stand or from the top of the tower, start with the default lens (1x) for the square and the buildings around it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole square in one frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out San Petronio or the distant towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Torre dell'Orologio (top of the clock tower, inside Palazzo d'Accursio on the Piazza Maggiore side). A bird's-eye view down onto the square and its surrounding buildings, with the sea of red rooftops and the towers beyond. The square lies to the east of you, ringed by San Petronio and the palaces. For a bird's-eye view, the top of the Torre dell'Orologio, the clock tower inside Palazzo d'Accursio on the west side, is a separate, ticketed alternative. From there the photo looks down onto the square and the buildings around it, with the red rooftops and towers stretching away beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. If you go up the tower, place the square in the lower half, with the rooftops and towers filling the upper half.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the square to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the rooftops keep their colour. Try a Live Photo for a bit of movement from the people crossing the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the rooftops best. Check the tower's opening times before you plan the visit.

text.access_note: The square itself is open to walk around, but the clock tower is a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.

name: Two Towers
label: Due Torri
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via Rizzoli' (5 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via Rizzoli nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/11986065: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Two Towers' (37 m across).
notes: The leaning Asinelli and Garisenda towers, symbol of Bologna.

text.description:
The Two Towers, the Asinelli and the Garisenda, are the symbol of Bologna, and Via Rizzoli gives the classic head-on view of them. From the portico you look east along the straight street, with both towers rising at the far end. The Garisenda's lean shows clearly against the sky next to its taller neighbour. This is the angle on most postcards. The long line of arches also gives you a natural frame.

The towers are traditionally credited to two local families and dated to between 1109 and 1119, though few documents survive to confirm it. The Asinelli now stands about 97 metres tall. The Garisenda is only about 48 metres, but it leans by around 3.2 metres. It was once much taller and was shortened in the 14th century when the ground beneath it gave way. Dante mentions it in his writing.

The Garisenda has been sealed off since October 2023 while work to stabilise it goes on, so you can only photograph it from outside. Barriers and fences may appear in your frame near the base, so it helps to shoot from further back along the street. Leave yourself a little time to try both portrait and landscape shots. For something different, Piazza di Porta Ravegnana at the foot of the towers lets you shoot upward, and Strada Maggiore shows the Asinelli between old façades.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, at the eastern end of Via Rizzoli, where the street meets Piazza di Porta Ravegnana and the towers stand.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stops are listed for this spot, so start from Piazza Maggiore and walk east along Via Rizzoli. The towers come into view at the end of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) held upright, so you can fit the Asinelli's full height and the Garisenda's lean in one shot. The default lens (1x) suits a tighter, cleaner view of the pair. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details, such as the top of the Asinelli or the tilt of the Garisenda.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via Rizzoli (from the portico, looking east toward the towers at the end of the street). Both towers rising at the far end of the straight porticoed street, with the Garisenda's lean visible against the sky. Under the portico, and face east toward the towers at the end of the street. From here you see both towers rising at the far end of the straight porticoed street, with the Garisenda's lean visible against the sky. For a low upward shot, walk on to Piazza di Porta Ravegnana. Strada Maggiore gives a quieter view of the Asinelli between old façades.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the street's centre line on the middle vertical line. Keep the phone level so the façades do not tilt inwards. Let the porticoes frame the left or right edge. The Garisenda's lean is the point of the picture, so keep it clear of fences and lampposts. If barriers get in the way, move to the other side of the street. Take a second shot from Piazza di Porta Ravegnana, pointing the phone upward.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the towers to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the brickwork stays visible. Take a few frames, because passers-by often walk through the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or evening, when the light is soft. In the evening, if the light fades, try night mode with the phone braced against a pillar of the portico.

text.access_note: Via Rizzoli is an ordinary public street. The Garisenda is closed to the public, and the Asinelli may or may not be open, so check on the day with Bologna Welcome or the comune before you go.

name: Basilica of San Petronio
label: San Petronio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Maggiore' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Maggiore' (relation/12719090): middle (161 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/328013918: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di San Petronio' (164 m across).
notes: Huge Gothic basilica with an unfinished marble facade.

text.description: The Basilica of San Petronio fills the south side of Piazza Maggiore, and its red-brick and marble front is one of the most recognisable sights in Bologna. It is dedicated to the city's patron saint, Saint Petronius, who was Bishop of Bologna in the fifth century. Work began in 1390. The main façade has never been finished, so its red brick and marble make a distinctive two-tone picture. The church is huge: about 132 metres long, 66 metres wide and 47 metres tall. The main doorway, the Porta Magna, carries carved scenes and figures by Jacopo della Quercia. That wide view is the classic postcard shot. Stay outside for the façade; there is plenty to see without going in. Early in the day the light is softer and the square is quieter, so you can get a clean frame without crowds in front of the doors. If you have time, walk round to Piazza del Nettuno for a second picture, with the bronze Neptune in the foreground and the basilica rising behind him.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, on the south side of Piazza Maggiore, the city's main square, with the surrounding palaces on the other sides.
text.directions_text: Make for Piazza Maggiore in the historic centre of Bologna. Stand on the square facing the church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade across the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the palaces and open space around it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Porta Magna carvings and the brick-and-marble join.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Maggiore (stand on the square facing the basilica, which sits on the south side of the piazza). The unfinished red-brick and marble façade filling the frame across the open square, with the surrounding palaces around it. Which sits on the south side of the piazza. From here the unfinished red-brick and marble façade fills the frame across the open square, with the palaces around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the façade with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean. Keep the phone level and leave a little space above the roof. Include some open square at the bottom to give a sense of scale. For a second option, Piazza del Nettuno gives you Giambologna's bronze Neptune in the foreground with the basilica behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a touch so the pale marble keeps its detail. Try panorama for the whole sweep of the square and palaces, holding the phone steady and level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before about 9 a.m. for an emptier square and softer light. Sunrise or sunset gives warm light on the façade.

text.access_note: The square is open public space; the basilica is a working church, so check the official site before you go if you want to step inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines help keep the vertical edges of a large building straight when photographed from a square.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in pale marble in bright light.
The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) lets you fit more of the square and surrounding palaces into the frame.

name: Sanctuary of Madonna di San Luca
label: Santuario San Luca
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Santuario della Madonna di San Luca' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28303288: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sanctuary of the Madonna of San Luca' (91 m across).

text.description:
The Sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca is a basilica on the forested hill of Colle della Guardia, about 300 metres above the city plain and just southwest of the historic centre. It is the reward at the end of the long climb from Bologna, and it photographs well for two reasons: the church itself is a handsome domed landmark, and the terrace beside it looks straight back over the city.

The phone icon on the map marks the sanctuary itself. The panoramic terrace and square lie at the back and side of the church, facing the city, so confirm the exact spot on arrival. From the terrace you can see Bologna's terracotta rooftops, the two towers and Piazza Maggiore spread across the plain, and on clear days the Apennines too. The arches around the terrace make natural frames for a phone shot.

The present church dates from 1723 and was designed by Carlo Francesco Dotti. The hill is also known for its covered arcade, a 3.8 km portico of 666 arches built between 1674 and 1793, which is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Porticoes of Bologna. A modern road also reaches the top.

For practical advice, take a wide view of the city first, then turn back for a second shot of the basilica's facade and dome from the open forecourt. Wipe your lens before you start, because a smudge shows up badly against a bright sky. Allow time for the climb and some wandering around the terrace.
text.geographic_location: The sanctuary stands on top of Colle della Guardia, just southwest of Bologna's historic centre, at the end of the long San Luca portico that starts at Porta Saragozza.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the historic centre of Bologna and head southwest towards the hill. A modern road and the covered San Luca portico both lead to the sanctuary. If you prefer to walk, the traditional way up is the portico from Porta Saragozza, which is a long climb. The phone icon on the map marks the sanctuary on the hilltop, and the map shows the spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the city view from the terrace. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the basilica from the forecourt, so the facade and dome fit in from close up. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the two towers and Piazza Maggiore in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Confirm the exact spot on arrival, then stand on the terrace facing the city. From there your view takes in the terracotta rooftops, the two towers and Piazza Maggiore across the plain.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the arches around the terrace as a frame: stand a little way back and let them surround the view of the city. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the rooftops in the lower half and plenty of sky above. For a second picture, walk to the open forecourt and photograph the full facade and dome above the wide steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the rooftops don't wash out. Try panorama mode to sweep across the whole plain, moving slowly and keeping the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is the time most guides recommend for the city view. Late afternoon gives warm light on the basilica's facade.

text.access_note: The terrace and square are open public space, but the church is a place of worship and its interior may be restricted or closed for restoration, so check the official site before you go.

name: Fountain of Neptune
label: Fountain of Neptune
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Nettuno' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Nettuno' (relation/4277749): middle (104 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/561636974: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fontana del Nettuno' (12 m across).
notes: Giambologna's bronze fountain beside Piazza Maggiore.

text.description: The Fountain of Neptune stands in Piazza del Nettuno, right beside Piazza Maggiore, and is one of the best-known symbols of Bologna. A large bronze Neptune rises from a marble basin, with his left arm stretched out as if calming the waves. Below him, four Nereids on the base hold their breasts, with water jets coming from them, and small cherubs hold dolphins. The fountain was designed by Tommaso Laureti and finished in 1565, and the bronze figure by Giambologna was fixed in place around 1566. It was commissioned by Cardinal Legate Charles Borromeo to celebrate his uncle's election as Pope Pius IV. It works well on a phone because the statue is tall, dark and clearly outlined, and the setting changes a lot depending on where you point the camera. The classic picture is Neptune in front of the bulk of the Basilica di San Petronio, which guides recommend as the shot that reads as Bologna. If you walk round to the Piazza Maggiore side of the basin, you can see how the jets frame the statue. In the evening, the tower of Palazzo d'Accursio makes a good backdrop when it is lit. Older photos show a darker, greener bronze, because the fountain was restored in 2016-2017. The square is free to enter, but early service vehicles and cleaning machines cross it, so keep an eye out and stay out of the main flow of walkers.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, in Piazza del Nettuno, which sits next to Piazza Maggiore.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Piazza Maggiore in the middle of the old town. Piazza del Nettuno is the square right beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic framing of Neptune with the Basilica di San Petronio behind. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole basin and the jets in the frame, but keep the statue away from the edges so it does not stretch. A telephoto lens (2x-5x) is useful for the face, the trident and the outstretched hand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno (Piazza Maggiore side of the basin). Neptune in front of the bulk of the Basilica di San Petronio behind him, the classic Bologna postcard framing. For the classic Bologna postcard view of Neptune in front of the bulk of the Basilica di San Petronio, move to the Piazza Maggiore side of the basin. Walking round the basin from that side also shows how the jets frame the statue. Check the side views on the day.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the vertical lines, with the basilica filling the space behind him when you are on the Piazza Maggiore side. Keep the phone level so the verticals stay straight. For something different, try the tower of Palazzo d'Accursio as a backdrop in the evening. There is also a spot where Neptune's outstretched thumb lines up with his body, giving the 'stone of shame' joke; for that, crouch low and shoot from the stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the dark bronze keeps its detail against the bright sky. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid edge. If the jets are running, a Live Photo can catch the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before about 9 a.m., when the square is nearly empty; shortly after sunrise also works. In the evening, the lit tower of Palazzo d'Accursio makes a good backdrop.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, free and open at all hours.

name: Portico of San Luca
label: Portico di San Luca
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arco del Meloncello' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Arco del Meloncello' (way/488692649): middle (14 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28303288: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sanctuary of the Madonna of San Luca' (91 m across).
notes: The world's longest portico, leading up to San Luca.

text.description:
The Portico of San Luca is a covered arcade of 666 arches that climbs from Porta Saragozza, one of Bologna's old city gates, up Colle della Guardia to the Sanctuary of the Madonna of San Luca. It is about 3.8 km long and was built between 1674 and 1793 to shelter the yearly procession carrying the icon of the Virgin Mary between the sanctuary and the cathedral. It is widely described as the longest portico in the world, and since 2021 it has been part of the UNESCO listing for the Porticoes of Bologna.

It photographs well because the same arch repeats again and again and the line of them leads your eye uphill towards the sanctuary. From there you look up the covered walkway as it climbs the hillside, with the arches receding into the distance. It comes early in the climb, so it is easy to reach. If you want a second angle, Porta Saragozza gives a leading-line view of the first stretch of arches. The sanctuary forecourt gives a wide view over the wooded hills and the city, with the dome in the frame.

The whole walk is long and uphill, so wear sensible shoes and check the weather. Early morning is usually the softest light and the quietest time.
text.geographic_location: The portico runs through the south-western edge of Bologna, from Porta Saragozza on the edge of the historic centre up the wooded Colle della Guardia. The Arco del Meloncello is on the lower part of the climb, and the sanctuary sits on the hilltop.
text.directions_text: No station, tram stop or other public transport is listed for this spot, so start from Bologna's historic centre and walk to Porta Saragozza, then follow the portico uphill to the Arco del Meloncello. Walking the whole arcade from the centre takes roughly an hour. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the arch and the portico climbing away from it. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to squeeze the arches together so they look like a stack receding up the hill. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the arch to fill the frame, and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Arco del Meloncello. Looking up the covered portico as it climbs the hillside, with its repeating arches receding toward the sanctuary. The covered portico climbs away to the south-west towards the sanctuary, and the repeating arches recede into the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the middle of the walkway on the central vertical line, so the arches converge symmetrically. Wait for a gap between walkers, or include one person for scale. For a different angle, try the first stretch of arches at Porta Saragozza, or the view over the city from the sanctuary forecourt.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far arches to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright opening at the far end doesn't wash out. A Live Photo can help you pick a frame with no one walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is suggested for softer light and fewer people. The climb is long, so allow time and check the weather first.

text.access_note: The portico is a public covered walkway and the view from the sanctuary forecourt is open-air, but for the church, the dome and any paid terrace, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The portico is a public walkway that can be photographed from outside without a ticket.
The far end of a covered arcade can look brighter than the arches around you, so lowering the exposure slider can help.
Using a telephoto lens (2x-5x) makes repeating arches look more tightly stacked than the default lens (1x).

label: Pinacoteca Nazionale

notes: The main art gallery of Bologna.

text.description: The Pinacoteca Nazionale is Bologna's national art gallery. It sits in a former Jesuit novitiate, the Saint Ignatius building, which Alfonso Torreggiani designed in 1726. The same building also houses the Academy of Fine Arts. For a phone photographer the appeal is the building itself: a calm, dignified façade in the University district, away from the busiest squares. It suits a record shot of your visit, or a quiet architectural frame. The collection inside covers Emilian painting from the 13th to the 18th century. It includes Guido Reni's Massacre of the Innocents. The gallery has been open to the public on a regular basis since 1875, and it also runs temporary exhibitions. Outside, start with the whole front in one frame, then move closer for details such as doorways, windows and stonework. Keep your phone upright for tall façades and sideways if you want the street included. Inside, photography rules differ from room to room and can change, so check the official site before you go and follow the signs and staff.
text.geographic_location: In Bologna's University district, on via delle Belle Arti (number 56). The gallery shares its building with the Academy of Fine Arts.
text.directions_text: From the University district, walk to via delle Belle Arti and look for number 56. If you are coming from further away, head to the University district and walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so there is no extra walk once you reach the address. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the façade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit the whole building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The building is directly there, so step back along the pavement as far as is safe to fit more of it in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them so the walls do not lean. Take one wide shot of the whole front, then a closer one of a doorway or window. Use the telephoto (2x or more) for details higher up the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Keep the phone level so the lines stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the façade is evenly lit. On a bright day, early or late sun gives softer shadows on the walls.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go for opening arrangements and photography rules inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The street in front of the building may be narrow, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may help to fit the whole building in.
Photography rules inside museum rooms vary and can change.
The façade is evenly lit in daytime, and early or late sun gives softer shadows.
The University district is quieter than the busiest central squares.

name: Giardini Margherita
label: Giardini Margherita
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chalet dei Giardini Margherita' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Chalet dei Giardini Margherita' (node/687861253): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23296119: large area 'Giardini Margherita' (924 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Largest and most popular city park of Bologna.

text.description:
Giardini Margherita is Bologna's big city park, just south of the centre, and the lake is its best subject for a phone. From the Chalet dei Giardini Margherita you look across the pond to the banks, the trees and the curving water path, and the far end of the lake sits neatly in the frame. That gives you water in the foreground, layers of green behind it and plenty of room for reflections.

The park opened on 6 July 1879. The city bought land that had belonged to an ancient convent, and the design by Ernesto Baldo Bertone di Sambuy is a typical English landscape garden. That is why it feels relaxed rather than formal. In the main square there is also a liberty-style building that was used for many years as an astronomical observatory, which makes a good second photo if you stroll further.

For your phone, keep the shot simple: let the water path lead the eye towards the far end of the lake, and keep the horizon level using the gridlines. If you want a different view, San Michele in Bosco looks down over the park's trees and the red roofs and towers of the city centre, with the Basilica of San Petronio visible. There the park is only the foreground, so it works better as a city panorama than as a park picture.
text.geographic_location: Giardini Margherita lies just south of Bologna's city centre. The lakeside Chalet is inside the park, on the shore of the small lake.
text.directions_text: From the city centre, head south towards the park; it lies just south of the centre. Once inside, follow the paths to the lake and look for the Chalet dei Giardini Margherita. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view across the pond. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more trees and sky, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the far end of the lake.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Chalet dei Giardini Margherita (lakeside, looking across the pond from the Chalet terrace). The park's small lake with its banks, trees and the curving water path, with the lake's far end visible in the frame. From here the photo shows the park's small lake with its banks, trees and the curving water path, with the far end of the lake in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water edge on the lower line, with the path curving into the frame. Keep the far end of the lake visible so the picture has depth. For a second viewpoint, San Michele in Bosco gives a wider view over the treetops and city roofs, but the park is a smaller part of that picture.

name: Palazzo d'Accursio
label: Palazzo d'Accursio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Maggiore' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Maggiore' (relation/12719090): middle (161 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/149040859: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo d'Accursio' (96 m across).

text.description:
Palazzo d'Accursio is Bologna's town hall, and it forms the western side of Piazza Maggiore, the city's main square. It began as the home of the jurist Accursius, then grew by taking in neighbouring buildings. In 1336 it became the seat of the Anziani, the commune's senior magistrates. In the 15th century the architect Fioravante Fioravanti added the clock tower. The palace now also holds the Civic Art Collection, the Museo Morandi and the Biblioteca Salaborsa.

It photographs well because the long stone façade, with its coats of arms and terracotta-coloured clock tower, sits behind a wide open square, so you can step back and fit a lot in. Look for the Madonna and Child in terracotta by Niccolò dell'Arca (1478) high on the front, and the large bronze statue of Pope Gregory XIII (1580) above the doorway. These make good close-ups once you have your wide shot.

It is on the square's west side near the Fontana del Nettuno, with the palace to the north-west. Keep the phone level so the façade doesn't lean, and wait for a gap in the crowd before you shoot. If you go inside, photography rules in some rooms may differ, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, on the western edge of Piazza Maggiore, close to the Fontana del Nettuno. The palace is the city's town hall.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Piazza Maggiore is in the historic centre of Bologna and can be reached on foot. From there the palace is about 1 minute on foot to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole façade and clock tower across the square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock tower, the coats of arms and the statue over the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Maggiore (west side of the square, near the Fontana del Nettuno). The palace's stone façade, with its coats of arms and terracotta clock tower, framed across the main square. From here the palace lies to the north-west, and you see its stone façade with the coats of arms and the terracotta clock tower framed across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the façade up with the horizontal lines so the building doesn't tilt. Leave some open square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. Then zoom in on the clock tower and the sculpture above the portal for detail shots. For a quieter alternative, try Via Carbonesi, where the clock tower can be seen from a side street away from the square's crowds. Check that view on the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone and terracotta keep their colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekday mornings tend to be quieter, and late afternoon gives warm, golden light.

name: Bologna Cathedral
label: Bologna Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Via dell'Indipendenza' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of Via dell'Indipendenza nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/325434925: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Cattedrale di San Pietro' (113 m across).
notes: The cathedral of Bologna on Via dell'Indipendenza.

text.description:
Bologna Cathedral, the Metropolitan Cathedral of Saint Peter, is the seat of the city's archbishop. Most of what you see dates from the 17th century, with a few parts older. The street front is later: the Baroque façade was added between 1743 and 1747 to designs by Alfonso Torreggiani, on the instructions of Pope Benedict XIV. A cathedral has stood on this spot since at least 1028, and its round-based bell tower is the second tallest in Bologna after the Asinelli Tower.

The church is tall and sits right on a narrow street, so it is hard to fit in one frame. That is also what makes it interesting to photograph: you get strong vertical lines, carved stone and deep shadows under the arcades. Check the exact portico position on site. Expect a fairly tight view from here. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the whole front, or the default lens (1x) for the central part. If you want a detail, such as the upper windows or the stonework, switch to the telephoto. Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level, so the building doesn't lean backwards. Use the arches beside you as a natural frame. If the full façade won't fit, a deliberately close crop looks better than a squeezed one.
text.geographic_location: Bologna Cathedral stands on Via dell'Indipendenza, in the historic centre of Bologna. The street is lined with porticoes, and the cathedral's Baroque front faces it.
text.directions_text: Head for Via dell'Indipendenza in the centre of Bologna; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for the Cattedrale di San Pietro. From there the cathedral lies to the east, about 1 minute on foot from its doors. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to get as much of the façade in as the narrow street allows. Then try the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the centre. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the upper façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Via dell'Indipendenza (under the porticoes on the cathedral side of the street, facing the baroque façade). The Baroque front of San Pietro seen across the street from the arcades, though framed fairly tightly. Check the exact portico position on site. You are quite close, so the front fills the frame and you can't step far back.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the portico arches as a frame at the edge of the picture. Switch on gridlines and line up the façade's vertical edges with them, holding the phone as level as you can, because tilting up makes the building lean. If the whole front won't fit, fill the frame with the central part instead. If the bell tower appears in frame, you can include it in a wider shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, as it is hard to judge the best crop on the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the afternoon and early evening, when the sun is likely to reach the west-facing front. Early morning is usually quieter on the pavement.

text.access_note: The street and its porticoes are public, but the cathedral is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress code.
claims_not_in_sources: The façade faces west onto the street, so it is likely to catch the sun in the afternoon and evening (inferred from the 'west front' in the sources).
The street is narrow and busy with pedestrians, so the pavement under the porticoes may be crowded at times.
Early morning is usually quieter.
Tilting the phone upwards makes the building's vertical lines lean inwards.
Visitors to the cathedral are usually expected to dress modestly.

name: Porta Saragozza
label: Porta Saragozza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza di Porta Saragozza' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza di Porta Saragozza' (way/82549440): point nearest the subject (127 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/241123644: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Porta Saragozza' (42 m across).
notes: Medieval city gate at the start of the San Luca portico.

text.description:
Porta Saragozza is one of Bologna's old city gates, built into the medieval walls in the 13th and 14th centuries. By 1334 it had a drawbridge over a moat. For a long time it saw little traffic. That changed in 1674, when the long Portico di San Luca was built to link the city centre with the Basilica of San Luca. The gate became the start of the yearly procession carrying the sacred icon, and was also known as the Porta Sacra or Porta dei Pellegrini (Holy Gate or Gate of the Pilgrims). Its present castle-like look dates from 1859, when the architect Giuseppe Mengoli joined two crenellated arches to the two round towers either side.

It photographs well because the whole gate fits in one frame: red brick, two sturdy towers and crenellations, with open space around it. Stand there and the gate sits straight ahead, with room for the sky above. For a different picture, walk up to the gate and shoot the arches and stonework, or look back through the passage towards the city. Another option is to frame the gate at the end of Via Saragozza, with the houses and walls either side. Traffic and passers-by can wander into the shot, so take a few frames and pick the cleanest.
text.geographic_location: Porta Saragozza stands in the line of Bologna's medieval walls, where Via Saragozza reaches the gate and the Portico di San Luca begins. The square in front of it is on the city side.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Bologna, walk to Piazza di Porta Saragozza, or follow Via Saragozza on foot until the gate appears at the end of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the square to get both towers and the arch between them. If you are close and the towers are cut off, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the crenellations and brick detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza di Porta Saragozza (in front of the gate, on the city-side approach). The full red-brick gate with its two towers and crenellations, framed by the open square. In front of the gate on the city-side approach. From here you see the full red-brick gate with its two towers and crenellations, framed by the open square. For a second shot, go to the gate itself for the arches and stonework, or to Via Saragozza for the gate at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines so they don't lean. Keep the gate centred, with a little sky and a little square around it. From Via Saragozza, let the houses on either side lead the eye to the gate. Under the arch, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) or the default lens (1x) to catch the passage and the view back towards the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo if people are walking through, then choose the frame with the clearest view of the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the brick and fewer people in the square. At midday, with the gate to the south of you, the sun is behind it, so tap on the brickwork and lower the exposure.

text.access_note: The gate and the square in front of it are in the open street, but access to the towers or any viewing area is not confirmed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the square.
With the gate to the south of the photographer, midday sun is behind the gate, so the brickwork may look dark unless exposure is adjusted.
Traffic and passers-by may enter the frame near the gate.
Access to the towers or any viewing area is not confirmed and may be restricted or ticketed.

name: Santo Stefano
label: Santo Stefano
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Santo Stefano' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Santo Stefano' (way/23296399): middle (132 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1192911978: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di Santo Stefano' (56 m across).
notes: The complex of the Seven Churches on a charming square.

text.description:
Santo Stefano is not one church but a cluster of linked religious buildings, which Bolognese people call the Sette Chiese, or Seven Churches. Tradition says Saint Petronius, a 5th-century bishop of the city, founded it on the site of a temple of Isis, wanting a place that recalled the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. The oldest parts date back to the 4th and 5th centuries, while the Courtyard of Pilate, the cloister-like space inside, is 13th-century.

The best phone photo is the view along Piazza Santo Stefano. This is a wedge-shaped square, wide at one end and narrowing towards the basilica. The porticoed palazzi on both sides lead the eye straight to the brick façade, so the church sits neatly at the centre of the frame. Guides often call it the most photogenic square in Bologna, and this is the view most people come for.

Put yourself at the wide end of the square, and face east. The basilica is only a short step away, so you can take the photo in a minute. If you go inside, look for signs about photography first, as it may be restricted in the churches. The square is a busy pedestrian area, particularly at weekends and in the evening, so a quiet morning gives you the cleanest picture.
text.geographic_location: Santo Stefano stands on Piazza Santo Stefano in Bologna, with the basilica closing the narrow end of the square and the porticoed palazzi lining both sides.
text.directions_text: No Underground, railway or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map to reach Piazza Santo Stefano in Bologna and finish on foot. The square is pedestrian, so go the last stretch on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the church with the palazzi on each side much as your eye sees it. If the square feels cramped, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to include more of the porticoes, but keep the phone level so the buildings don't lean. For the Courtyard of Pilate or brick details on the façade, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Santo Stefano (wide end of the triangle, facing the basilica). The brick basilica fills the frame at the apex, with the porticoed palazzi on both sides funnelling the eye toward it. At the wide end of the triangle, facing the basilica to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the church on the centre line, with the portico edges running into the frame on either side. Keep the phone level, and wait for a gap in the passers-by if you want an empty square. For a different view, the Cortile di Pilato inside the complex gives arches, worn stone and pools of light and shadow.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brick façade to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick keeps its colour. Use portrait mode only for a person standing in the square, not for the church itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is best: the low sun crosses the piazza and there are fewer people. Late afternoon or evening also works for golden-hour light, although the square is busier then.

text.access_note: The square is an open pedestrian space, but for the churches and courtyard inside, and for any rules on photography there, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The basilica sits in a pedestrian area.
From the wide end of Piazza Santo Stefano the basilica is to the east.
Early morning light crosses the square and gives fewer crowds; late afternoon and evening give golden-hour light.
The square is busier at weekends and in the evening.

name: Palazzo Re Enzo
label: Palazzo Re Enzo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza del Nettuno' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza del Nettuno' (relation/4277749): middle (104 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/149040903: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palazzo Re Enzo' (78 m across).
notes: 13th-century palace where King Enzo was held prisoner.

text.description: Palazzo Re Enzo is a medieval brick palace on Piazza del Nettuno in Bologna's historic centre, and it suits a phone camera well. Its battlements, plain brick walls and open loggia give strong lines and texture. From Piazza del Nettuno the Neptune Fountain sits in the foreground, which adds depth, and the Palazzo del Podestà stands alongside. The palace was built between 1244 and 1246 as an extension of the Podestà building, which had become too small for the city's government, and it was first called the "New Palace". It takes its name from Enzio of Sardinia, son of Emperor Frederick II, who was held here as a prisoner from 1249 until he died in 1272. Its Gothic look today comes largely from a restoration in 1905 by Alfonso Rubbiani, so you are seeing a carefully revived medieval style. Inside, the palace is used for cultural events and exhibitions. For photographs, the exterior is what matters. Stand on the west side of the square, facing the entrance, and let the fountain fill the lower part of the frame with the brick façade rising behind it. For something quieter, walk round to Piazza Re Enzo for the back and side of the palace, with its medieval tower and the large pointed arches leading under the Voltone. Check the palace is not covered in scaffolding before you go, as restoration work can spoil the view.
text.geographic_location: Palazzo Re Enzo is in the historic centre of Bologna, on Piazza del Nettuno, right beside the Palazzo del Podestà and the Neptune Fountain.
text.directions_text: Head for the historic centre of Bologna and aim for Piazza del Nettuno. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the fountain and the palace front look natural together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the façade will not fit, and try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the battlements and brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza del Nettuno (west side, facing the palace's entrance and the Neptune Fountain). The palace's brick façade and battlements, with the Neptune Fountain in the foreground and the Palazzo del Podestà alongside. On the west side, facing the palace's entrance and the Neptune Fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the fountain low in the frame, with the brick façade and battlements above it. Keep the phone level so the vertical walls do not lean. For a different view, Piazza Maggiore shows the palace among the neighbouring medieval buildings and the Basilica di San Petronio. Piazza Re Enzo gives the quieter back and side, with the tower and the big pointed arches over the Voltone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the façade keeps its colour. With the telephoto, hold the phone steady with both hands, elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Try the afternoon or early evening, when the façade is likely to catch warm light. Go early in the morning if you want fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The exterior and the square can be photographed from public space, but inside the palace is open only for events and exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.

The square is usually quieter early in the morning than later in the day.
Piazza del Nettuno is open public space that can be visited at any time.

name: Basilica of San Domenico
label: San Domenico
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza San Domenico' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza San Domenico' (relation/15876409): middle (154 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/328022875: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Basilica di San Domenico' (140 m across).
notes: Church holding the tomb of Saint Dominic.

text.description: The Basilica of San Domenico is one of Bologna's major churches, and its square is the easiest place to photograph it from. The Romanesque facade dates from 1240 and was restored in 1910. Its large rose window is the centrepiece of the picture. The square is paved with pebbles, as it was in medieval times, and it holds several things that work as foreground detail. There is a column with a bronze statue of St Dominic (1627) and a second column topped by the Madonna of the Rosary (1632), put up after a design by Guido Reni to mark the end of a plague. There are also two medieval tombs: Rolandino de' Passeggeri (1305) and Egidio Foscarari (1289). Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominicans, died in the church on 6 August 1221, and his remains rest inside in an elaborate shrine worked on by several artists, including the young Michelangelo. For a phone photo, stand back in the square and let a statue or tomb sit low in the frame, with the facade and rose window behind it. That gives the picture depth and shows how the square and church belong together. If you go inside, the interior is Baroque, but check the official site before you go for visiting times and photography rules.
text.geographic_location: In the university city of Bologna, Italy, in Piazza San Domenico, directly in front of the basilica's facade.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or journey planner for the way to Piazza San Domenico. The basilica itself is about 1 minute on foot to the south-east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole facade and a statue or tomb in front of it. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the rose window and the Madonna statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza San Domenico (in front of the basilica facade). The Romanesque facade with its rose window, lit by afternoon sun, with the tombs and statues of the square in the foreground. From here the basilica lies to the south-east. You see the Romanesque facade with its rose window, and the tombs and statues of the square in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the edges of the facade up with the vertical lines, so the building doesn't lean. Place a statue or tomb in the lower part of the frame and the rose window in the upper part. If you want a quieter alternative, the cloister inside the complex has arcades and architectural lines that suit a straight-on shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail in bright light. Keep your phone level to avoid converging verticals. Panorama is rarely needed here; the ultra-wide lens does the job more simply.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Afternoon, when the light falls on the facade and the Madonna statue.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica and its cloister are a place of worship and a visitor site, so check the official site before you go for opening times and photography rules.

name: Palazzo del Podestà
label: Palazzo del Podestà
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Maggiore' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Maggiore' (relation/12719090): middle (161 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/149040794: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Salone della Podestà' (74 m across).
notes: Renaissance palace with a tall tower on Piazza Maggiore.

text.description:
The Palazzo del Podestà is a long civic building on Piazza Maggiore, facing the Basilica di San Petronio and close to the Palazzo Comunale. It was built around 1200 as the seat of the podestà, the commune's officials. In 1245 the Palazzo Re Enzo was added alongside it, topped by the Torre dell'Arengo, whose bell was rung to call people together in emergencies. In 1453 Aristotile Fioravanti rebuilt the old Gothic facade in Renaissance style for Giovanni II Bentivoglio.

It photographs well because the whole front can be seen across the open square, with the brick-and-sandstone facade and the tower together in one frame. The ground floor is a double open arcade, the Voltone del Podestà, with two lanes of shops running through it. Terracotta statues of the city's protectors were placed there in 1525. These make good close-up details.

Start with a wide shot to show the palazzo and its tower, with San Petronio nearby. Then step in for details such as the arches, the brickwork and the statues. If you want a different angle, try framing the square through the vaulted Voltone, or go to Piazza Re Enzo for a quieter view back towards Piazza Maggiore, with the palazzo at the left of the frame.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Bologna, on the Piazza Maggiore. It stands near the Palazzo Comunale, opposite the Basilica di San Petronio and beside the Palazzo Re Enzo.
text.directions_text: Head for Piazza Maggiore in the historic centre of Bologna. The palazzo is directly north of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the wide view of the facade and tower across the square. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot fit the whole front in, and to 2x or more for the arches, statues and brick and sandstone textures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Maggiore (north side of the square, facing the palazzo's facade). The palazzo's brick-and-sandstone facade and tower framed across the open square, with the Basilica di San Petronio nearby. From here the brick-and-sandstone front and the tower are framed across the open square, with the Basilica di San Petronio nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the facade up with them so the building does not lean. Leave some open square in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a different shot, frame the square through the vaulted arcade of the Voltone del Podestà. Piazza Re Enzo gives a quieter view back towards Piazza Maggiore.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky stays blue and the sandstone keeps its detail. Try panorama mode only if you hold the phone upright and turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour is the best time, when the warm light suits the sandstone. In the evening, night mode helps if you hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The square is a free, open public space, but the palazzo's interior may only be open during exhibitions, so check the official site before you go.

name: San Giacomo Maggiore
label: San Giacomo Maggiore
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Piazza Rossini' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Piazza Rossini' (way/771824279): middle (74 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/554723325: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chiesa di San Giacomo Maggiore' (98 m across).
notes: Gothic church with a famous portico along Via Zamboni.

text.description:
San Giacomo Maggiore is a large Augustinian church in the middle of Bologna, and its facade is the best place to start. It is the oldest part of the building, with late-Romanesque proportions and tall pointed windows framed in pale Istrian stone, added in 1295. Building began in 1267, the church was finished in 1315, and it was consecrated in 1344.

From Piazza Rossini you see the facade head-on, with the pointed windows, the portal and the small statue niche near the top. That straight-on view makes a tidy, balanced phone photo. The brick bell tower, raised in 1471, and the long portico the Bentivoglio family added in 1477–1481 also belong to the story, so look for them if you want a wider scene.

If you have time for a second shot, Piazza Verdi shows the bell tower and the rounded apse rising above the neighbouring buildings. That profile is more distinctive than the facade. Via Zamboni gives you the long colonnade of the portico beside the brick flank of the church.

Keep your photos to the outside. Photography inside the church is officially banned, so enjoy the Bentivoglio Chapel with your eyes rather than your phone.
text.geographic_location: San Giacomo Maggiore stands in the old centre of Bologna, beside the Conservatorio Giovanni Battista Martini, which occupies part of the former monastery.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for central Bologna and then go by taxi or hired scooter to Piazza Rossini. The church lies to the north-east of it, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the head-on facade. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square feels tight and you want the whole front plus some sky. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pointed windows and the statue niche at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Piazza Rossini (in front of the main facade). The church's Gothic facade head-on, with its pointed windows, the portal and the small statue niche at the top. The church is to the north-east. From here you see the Gothic facade head-on, with its pointed windows, the portal and the small statue niche at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical edge of the facade up with a grid line, so the building does not lean. Stand square to the centre of the front for a symmetrical shot. Keep your phone level and avoid tilting it upwards, as tilting makes the walls lean inwards. For a second view, try Piazza Verdi for the bell tower and apse, or Via Zamboni for the portico.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check how the light falls on the facade when you arrive. Early in the day is usually calmer on the square.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the open square outside; photography inside the church is officially banned, and visiting hours and access may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Archiginnasio of Bologna
label: Archiginnasio
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1476981: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Old university seat with the wooden Anatomical Theatre.

text.description:
The Archiginnasio was the main building of the University of Bologna. Today it houses the city's municipal library and the old Anatomical Theatre. It was built very quickly: work began in February 1562 and it opened in October 1563, when Piazza Maggiore was being remodelled under papal orders. The aim was to bring the law schools and the schools of philosophy, medicine and the sciences under one roof.

It photographs well because of its long porch, about 139 metres of thirty arches on sandstone columns. The repeating arches give you strong lines that lead the eye along the street. Look closely at the walls as well. They carry some six thousand painted coats of arms, each one marking a student who was elected head of a student organisation. You will also see 17th-century busts of lecturers along the lower portico, and the arms of Bologna families such as the Bentivoglio and Pepoli.

For your phone, use the arches for perspective and the walls for detail. Stand under the portico, line up the columns with the gridlines, and then step in close to a single coat of arms or bust. The upper floor holds the Anatomical Theatre, a fir-wood amphitheatre from 1636 that was rebuilt after wartime bombing. Visitors are asked to leave bags at the entrance, so check the official site before you go to find out what you can photograph inside.
text.geographic_location: The Archiginnasio is in the historic centre of Bologna, in the area around Piazza Maggiore. The building has a long porch of thirty arches.
text.directions_text: No Underground, railway or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is right at the building, so use the map to find it and you can start shooting as soon as you reach the portico. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the long run of arches. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the columns and walls. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the coats of arms and busts up on the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stay under the portico and shoot along the arches, or step back a little and take the front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the arches do not lean. Shoot along the portico so the arches lead into the distance. Then move in close for one coat of arms or one bust as a detail shot. Try a portrait-mode shot of a friend framed by an arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the stonework and painted arms keep their colour. In the shade under the arches, use night mode if the phone offers it and hold still for a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is best for seeing the painted coats of arms clearly under the portico. Early morning or a softly overcast day usually means fewer people and gentler light on the arches.

text.access_note: The library and Anatomical Theatre are inside the building and may have their own access rules, so check the official site before you go.
